body_markdown:
It was sometime in the early ’80s when Dad spotted the ’57 at a local service station—when there was still such a place. The gentleman there had purchased the amazing pink Bel Air from the original owner and told us that the woman was a teacher and had ordered the car for herself. This probably explains the Canyon Coral-and-white two-tone paint and the Blue Flame Six under the hood. I think Dad paid $3500 for it.


That first year, I was given the chance to drive it around and show it off. I remember once we took it out of Portland and up to Timberline Lodge on Mt. Hood, but mostly we just cruised Cedar Hills Boulevard to the local hangout. After all, it was[Dad’s car](https://www.hagerty.com/media/member-stories/it-took-years-but-restoring-my-dads-54-chevy-bel-air-was-worth-the-wait/) .


Katy Nielsen


Katy Nielsen


Katy Nielsen


My dad, Kaare Nielsen, was a lifelong GM guy. I certainly inherited that preference. My first car was a 1963 Impala, followed by an El Camino and a couple Blazers.


After that first summer, the ’57 did not get out much. Dad would start it and take it out of the garage to admire it but he didn’t drive it anywhere. I was busy working and newly married. But I always told Dad it was going to be my car someday. About 10 years later, someday happened. One Christmas Eve, after a period of time when he threatened to sell it to make more room in the shop, Dad came to my front door and handed me the signed title. “Merry Christmas!” and “Big Pink” was mine at last.


Katy Nielsen


The following summer my then-husband Dave changed all the belts and hoses and put it a new battery. We drove[the Bel Air](https://www.hagerty.com/media/great-reads/reuniting-grandpa-mel-with-a-55-bel-air-his-california-dream/) short distances, such as to the nicest restaurant in town, but did not feel confident getting too far from home. Sadly, most people had to come over and hang out in the garage with us to see my beautiful car.


Katy Nielsen


Fast forward another 10 years… I was single again, moved to another part of town, and determined to make the ’57 road-worthy. I wasn’t sure how to find a knowledgeable mechanic that I could afford, but I just got lucky. Through work I met the person who could help: Dave Bailie is real car guy and he could not rest knowing the car was a garage queen. He wanted to see it running again as much as I did. Big Pink went to his shop for several months and when it came home it was purring like a kitten.


Now we cruise again. I am still very careful about where and when Big Pink travels. We stay off the freeway and never venture out at rush hour. But when we do hit the road, people can’t help but smile and wave—because it’s a totally original, unmolested pink ’57 Chevy Bel Air, and there aren’t too many of those around anymore.


Katy Nielsen
